Yes. 

The story is tightly unified and follows a clear, logical progression from beginning to end. Details introduced in the first half—such as the oppressive July heat, the mother's stoic pride, the unspoken dread of "arrangements," the recurring dialogue ("You're late"), and the jar of blackberry jam left behind—all directly set up the events and emotional payoff of the second half. Every scene and object (the washed mug put back in place, the rationed jam, the unwashed dishes at the end) serves the central theme of aging, quiet loneliness, and the unspoken ways the mother and child hold onto each other's presence.
